items.text: How can we expect other count ries to take the lead and
reduce their emissions when we do not do our fair share and basically we are effectively
freeloading?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: By following the lead that we have just given.

items.speaker: Moana Mackey
items.text: How can he say that we are doing more than other countries when
New Zealand’s inaction is in stark contrast  to the commitments made by our Pacific
Island neighbours; and why did New Zealand sign the Majuro Declaration at the Pacific
Islands Forum in September, a statement urging countries to set more ambitious
emissions reduction targets, an action that led Pacific Island leaders at the forum to
believe that New Zealand woul d come up with tougher target s than were currently in
place, when we clearly had no intention of doing anything of the sort?

items.speaker: Hon TIM GROSER
items.text: Well, first of all, we need to examine very carefully the
statements of these Pacific Island countri es in terms of the underlying numbers and
assumptions that they have put forward on th e table. New Zealand is  doing as much as
any member, in my opinion, of the annex 1 countries. New Zealand has spent something
like $600 million—I stand to be corrected on the precise number—with fast-start
financing, helping predominantly Pacific co untries move across to renewables and
lower their emissions. I think New Zealand is doing a great deal in the Pacific pursuant
to that declaration.
Public Safety—Street-based Prostitution
12. Le’aufa’amulia ASENAT I LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Police
items.text: What reports, if any, has she rece ived concerning public harassment and
intimidation from street prostitutes and their clients? Talofa lava. I would also like to
acknowledge Papali’itele Peter Fatialofa’s family, who are farewelling him today at a
funeral service in Manukau.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I have not received any specific reports
about public harassment and intimidation from st reet prostitutes and their clients. As I
advised the House when the member asked a similar question in September, I have
received two reports regarding the Manukau City Council (Regulation of Prostitution in
Specified Places) Bill. Both of these reports  contained some comment on street-based
sex workers in South Auckland.
13 Nov 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14629
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : Does she believe that a prostitute and their
seedy client having sex in the yard of a private citizen constitutes a valid and legal
business transaction; if so, why?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Well, I have no responsibility for that, but I am aware of a
situation in Christchurch, and I have symp athy with the house ow ners. I do not think
that anyone wants to have that happening in  their backyard. However, they must not
take the law into their own hands. Where th ey are concerned about unsavoury activities
happening in their property, they should ring the police immediately.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : What does the Minister have to say, given
her previous answer just before, to the re sidents of Manchester Street, Christchurch,
who are having to shield their children from prostitutes having sex on their street, in
front of their homes, and often on their own property?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, in so far as there is mini sterial responsibility, the Hon Anne
Tolley.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: What I can say to the member is that the police are well
aware of the concerns. They are working w ith the Prostitutes Collective and with the
Christchurch City Council, and they are trying  to encourage those pr ostitutes to operate
in a safer environment and a more appropriate environment. But I think it is pertinent to
note that street prostitution is not illegal.  I repeat again that if members of the
community are feeling harassed or intimidated, or this activity is impinging on their
own properties, then I encourag e those people not to take the law into their own hands
but to ring the police.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Supplementary question, Asenati Lole-Taylor.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor : Taylor. Sorry, I did not hear my surname
completely finished. I thought you did not finish—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member ask her supplementary question.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: I am trying. Why are th e police investigating
a homeowner who simply defended herself whilst trying to remove a prostitute from her
property?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: My understanding is that a complaint was laid with the
police and that the police are investigating that complaint, as I would expect them to do.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I move, That the House take
note of miscellaneous business . We had some discussion about referenda in question
time, and it is pretty important to note that the Prime Minister, who obviously is not
very impassioned about this topic, had a couple of brain fades. The smacking
referendum was held in 2009 a nd the result was ignored by his Government. He struck
the deal with Helen Clark that resulted in the anti-smacking bill being passed, and he
and the entire National caucus voted for it.  A march against John Key’s decision to
ignore the referendum was sponsored to  the tune of $450,000 by guess who. “Crazy
Colin Craig”—“Crazy Colin Craig”. That has become deliciously ironic because now, 4
years later, “Desperate and Dateless John Key” is turning back to the very same “Crazy
Colin Craig”.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: He’s Nigel-no-mates.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Nigel-no-mates he is. John  Banks is in court, Peter
Dunne is in limbo, Pita and Tariana are on life support, and John Key will do a deal
with whomever he can to hang on in power, ev en if it is “Crazy Colin Craig”, the Sarah
Palin of New Zealand politics.
In fact, in September 2012 Colin Craig sent 20,000 leaflets to Helensville residents,
telling them that John Key was—wait for it—“too gay” to be their MP. Why would
14630 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
John Key want to go into partnership, sh all we say, with somebody who thought that
that was an insult?

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: It’s an uncivil union.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Exactly—an uncivil union. Bill English said that he did
not understand what Mr Craig’s economic polic y was. Well, we have researched this,
and we can tell you that Colin Craig is a supporter of—and it is the only sensible thing
he has ever said—a capital gains tax. Colin Craig wants a capital gains tax. He also
wants a binding referendum. So if John Ke y wants to do a date with “Crazy Colin
Craig”, let us make the asse t sales referendum binding, shall we? Let us make the asset
sales referendum binding.
Mr Craig has some very interesting views.  He has got an environmental policy, all
right. He thinks climate change is cause d by sunspots and the circulation of the
planets—sunspots and the circulation of the planets. It woul d be funny if it were not for
his views on social policy. Here we go. Follo wing a series of items about child poverty
on current affairs shows, Mr Craig said that children sent to school without lunch should
go without and, instead, their “delinquent” parents should be charged the “cost of
rectifying their bad behaviour”.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: That’ll work.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: That will work. He has views on social policy, which is
very topical. Mr Craig, of course, thinks that New Zealand has the most promiscuous
young women in the world. So John Key has got his work cut—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: How does he know?

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: How does he know? How does he know?
Poor Peter Dunne. Imagine how Peter Dunne  feels, being passed over for “Crazy
Colin Craig”.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: He’ll go away.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Exactly. Imagine how bad he feels. As if John Banks was
not enough. John Banks is in court, facing terrible retribution, and probably being
thrown out of Parliament, and he is going to be reinstated by John Key, but Peter Dunne
is not. Strike one—strike one. Now John Key wants to go on a date with “Crazy Colin
Craig”—strike two. What has Peter Dunne got  to do to worm his way back into John
Key’s good books? It is very, very hard to imagine.
Of course, the result of this shambles is that Nats are jumping off the sinking ship. In
fact, “like Nats off a sinking ship” has beco me a little bit of a phrase around here. Chris
Tremain—hundreds of real estate  signs in Napier showcase his name, but even that
could not save him. We like you, mate; sorr y you are going. But it is a stampede. Chris
Auchinvole lost the Coast, now he is a list MP, and now he is gone. Phil Heatley paid
for the wine with his mini sterial job. Paul Hutchis on—one can only wonder “whay”.
Cam Calder—one can only wonder who. Kate Wilkinson—apparently, she is going to
run in Christchurch East. Oh no, that was Mr Doocey—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: Hon CRAIG FOSS
items.text: What an admission of defeat that
was—the Leader of the Opposition, the part y on 32 percent, spending his 5 minutes
talking about a party that is not even in Parliament yet. The 32 percent party talking
about a party on 2 percent. It may be inte resting, but I would ha ve thought that the
Leader of the Opposition would spend his time putting up Labour’s policies as an
alternative to the very good policies of this Government. I was very surprised by that.
It was just 5 short years ago—just 5 short years ago—that New Zealand
overwhelmingly elected the John Key - led Na tional Party to lead the next National
Government with our coalition partners. We have spent those 5 years repairing,
rebuilding, and refocusing our shattere d economy—repairing, rebuilding, and
13 Nov 2013 General Debate 14631
refocusing confidence in New Zealand, and trying to build. We are succeeding now, but
the work continues with Better Public Se rvices, which is building and bringing in
policies that matter to New Zealanders in thei r homes and in their families. That is not
the PC nonsense that just 5 years ago so  preoccupied the members opposite, many of
whom are still on their front bench.
The National Party, in the 5 years we have thus far been in Government, has been
constantly putting in policies to create real  jobs and to create real wage growth for
families in New Zealand. We must note that  Labour and the Greens have voted against
every single one of those policies. The Nati onal Party is the party of jobs. The National
Party is the party for families. Every single one  of the policies we have put in place to
help their circumstances at their level has been voted against by Labour and the Greens,
which are forever preoccupied with their PC nonsense and all sorts of interesting things
that may be of interest in the beltway or to their caucuses. It is Better Public Services
that has brought in national standards in  education, aiming for a better educational
outcome for five out of five  of our New Zealand children. There are better outcomes in
health, with more electives than ever. Ther e are better policies on law and order, which
have led to a reduction in crime, particularly in violent crime.
Amazingly, it takes the National-led Government to bring in better policies for the
environment, such as freshwater standards.  One would have thought that the Greens
would promote that a wee bit when they were making arrangements with the Labour
Government last time. National is not only th e party for jobs for families; National is
also the party for the environment. We do not just talk about it; we do it. We take
action.
We are also enabling the regions to invest in  their future. We are the party for jobs in
the oil and gas industry. We are the party for jobs in water storage projects such as the
Ruataniwha scheme in Hawke’s Bay. I note that the Labour Party is against jobs in the
oil and gas industry. The Labour Party is agai nst the water storage project in Hawke’s
Bay.
Just 5 years ago Labour policies led to the decade of deficits. The best commentary I
have seen in quite a while of what 9 years of Labour meant was from John Armstrong in
the New Zealand Herald . When commenting on the Pre-el ection Economic and Fiscal
Update, he said: “The Treasury’s pre-elec tion economic and fiscal update bleeds so
much of the red stuff that the document l ooks like the aftermath of Dracula running
amok in the blood bank. The numbers in this  horror story are truly awful.” That was
commentary from a neutral observer after 9 years of the Labour Government.
The worry is that as bad as that all wa s, those policies are still unchanged in the
Labour-Greens Opposition. The policies are actually unchanged. The only new one I
know of is the printing money one, which I ha ve not heard about fo r a while, but that
still seems to be a policy. So the policies of the Labour Party that led to the decade of
deficits, the policies that led to rampant ta xation, lack of confid ence, and a ballooning
public sector, are still in its manifesto. It has not changed them. It may have renamed
them. It may have re-skinned them.
National is on track to achieve surplus ne xt year. National is on track to achieve
surplus in spite of the export recession over 5 of the years of the Labour Government, in
spite of the resultant recession for 1 year from 2008, in spite of the global financial
crisis, and in spite of the tr agedy and the tragic circumst ances around the Christchurch
earthquake. National is on track to achieve a better, brighter future. The work continues.
We cannot put it all at risk.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: On Friday I leave for Warsaw for the 19 th
annual meeting of the climat e negotiations. I was at the Earth Summit back in 1992
where all this kicked off. I was at the 16 th meeting in Copenhagen and the 18 th at Doha
14632 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
last year. It has been 20 years of struggle to save the planet from dangerous climate
change.
How have we done? The answer is not well, and the truth is that we are proving to be
inadequate to the task. The objective of the United Nati ons Framework Convention on
Climate Change is the stabilisation of gree nhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere
at a level that would prevent dangerous anthropogenic interferen ce with the climate
system. That year the level of global emi ssions was 38 billion t onnes. Today it is 50
billion tonnes, one-third highe r than when we undertook to reduce it. The UN says that
to stay under the 2 degree th reshold of a dangerous clim ate we must reduce global
emissions to 44 billion tonnes by 2020. Business as usual will see 56 billion tonnes of
emissions. Our voluntary pledges will also keep us way above the target.
The recent Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate
Change has four scenarios out to 2100. Only one scenario, requiring a radical mitigation
pathway, will keep us below the 2 degree thre shold. The other three scenarios project a
mean temperature rise of 2.6 degrees, 3 degr ees, or 4.5 degrees. Global warming to date
has been a rise of 0.8 degrees Celsius. We  see around us the extreme weather events
associated with a 0.8 degree rise—the fore st fires in Russia and Australia, and the
severe storms in America and the Philippines.  If this is what a 0.8 degree rise does,
imagine what a 3 or 4.8 degree rise will do—yet a 4.5 degree rise is business as usual.
Can we imagine what this will be? Why are we not factoring in the magnitude of this
threat in our political discourse?
Well, the people who are suffering from a 0.8 degree rise are doi ng just that. The
Philippines’ chief delegate at Warsaw had a few comments: “What my country is going
through as a result of this extreme climate event is madness. This climate crisis is
madness. We can stop this madness. Right he re in Warsaw. … We cannot sit and stay
helpless staring at this international climate stalemate. It is time to take action. We need
an emergency climate pathway.”
So Warsaw next week will test whether we  manage to get negotiations for a global
agreement back on track following the trai n wreck of Copenhagen and whether we
actually agree, as an international comm unity, to reduce global emissions from 50
billion tonnes to 44 billion tonnes by 2020, ju st 6 years away. If we do not, then, very
simply, we shall be committing our children to a catastrophic future.
How are we doing down here in New Zealand?  Are we doing our fair share in this
unprecedented and titanic task? New Zealand has the worst emissions record of all
OECD countries. Our net emissions have grown from 32 million tonnes back in 1992,
when we signed the convention and said we would start reducing them, to 57 million
tonnes today, a 78 percent increase. In 2020 they will be 70 million tonnes, and in 2028
they will be 96 million tonnes.
Does this bother our Prime Minister? No. When queried on the projected emissions
he offers a relaxed view of the future. Science, he says, will be “our friend” when it
comes to climate change. Science could “ quite possibly solve the problem of our
agricultural emissions”. Besides, New Zeala nders, he graciously observes, do not wish
to change: “I have never been of the view that people are going to  dramatically change
their lifestyle. They are not going to st op eating protein. They  are not going to stop
wanting New Zealand to produce that protein, but science can actually help us.”
It is wilful negligence of this kind that wi ll earn us, once again, the fossil awards at
Warsaw. This will enable Minister for Clim ate Changes Issues, Tim Groser, to jeer at
the global civil society, as he did in D oha, on the grounds that they are unrealistic
idealists who cannot perceive the real world for what it is. The truth is that the real
world is what the scientists, those friends of the Prime Minister, are describing it to be:
13 Nov 2013 General Debate 14633
catastrophic climate change in the course of  this century if we continue business as
usual in the manner that his Government, for incomprehensible reasons, wishes.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: There is a strange smell
that is starting to permeate across the Chambe r. It is the kind of smell one gets when
you walk across the high tide mark after a big storm. It is the kind of smell you get as
you walk through a forest. It is that smell of decay, of rot, of dead wood. Today the
Leader of the Opposition got to the heart of that. He backed up the rejuvenation that is
going on on this side of the House, as eight to 10 of our MPs make the decision to move
on to other things. We allow fresh, bright id eas to come into this party. On the other
side, though, the smell is permeating—that dead wood.
What we are seeing 5 years on from the st art of this Government is rejuvenation,
change, and new policy happening on this side  of the House. And on the other side?
Dead wood—dead wood policies and dead wo od politicians. When we come to the
election in just a few months’ time, toward s the end of next ye ar, the public will be
sitting there, saying: “What is on offer here? A party that after 6 years is bright with
new ideas and fresh people, or one that after 6 years has not changed. It is still full of
dead wood politicians.”
On that note I can say I wa s proud to attend the policy day up at Premier House, just
last Friday. We walked into Premier House— a caucus full of a huge vibe of confidence
and a resetting of our policies going forward. In that regard we talked long and hard
about the four key objectives that we set as a party when we came into office: firstly, to
return the Government’s books to surplus; secondly, to create a more productive and
competitive economy; thirdly, to build better public services; and, fourthly, to rebuild
that beautiful city of Christchurch, whic h I do not think anyone  in the House would
oppose. But in every one of those policy areas it was exciting to be able to talk about the
future, about new policies to add to those ones that have been implemented to date.
Let us have a look at some of the results th at we have achieved over the last 5 years
in regard to those key policy areas. There is  3 percent annual growth. That provides our
country with a huge future for children lik e mine, aged 17, 15, and 13, who are looking
to get into tertiary education and to go forward. An economy now with 3 percent growth
going forward is absolutely fantastic.
On top of that we are also going to set a path way to return to surplus. It is wonderful
to see the Labour spokesman on finance suppor ting that, and actually predicting that we
were going to do better than we ourselves th ought. I have got to say that that was
actually really good—a fantastic situation. Re turning to surplus, getting our accounts
back in order—a great thing. It is also good to see the IMF endorsement of the way we
are tracking. The accounts are in a good position moving forward.
Business confidence is strong, consumer c onfidence is really high, and immigration
has turned round from where we saw it. Ne t positive migration—in September alone an
additional 2,700 people moved to New Z ealand. More people are arriving than
departing. That is positive.
But what is best of all is that we are seeing the trend of unemployment continuing to
fall. This time last year unemployment was 7.2 percent. It got dow n to 6.4 percent, and
just in the September quarter it was down to 6.2 percent. We have still got work to do; I
accept that. But if we see that trend in economic growth continuing, that 2 to 3
percent—it is one of the best economies in the Western World—then I predict that next
year we will see that unemployment number  go down to the 5 percent range. So that is
absolutely fantastic.
Put that together with the new ideas that we were creating at Premier House last
Friday, and put that together with the re juvenation of our caucus, strong new faces
coming in, with fresh, positive ideas—what that presents is a party that is going into the
14634 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
next election with a spring in its step. Compare that with the Opposition—a bunch of
dead wood politicians with dead wood policies, going nowhere and offering no future in
any capacity to New Zealand. If I was the Leader of the Opposition, I would be worried,
with the polls going nowhere north anytime soon and with a caucus full of dead wood
politicians.
We understand that we are in a great position heading up to that election. It is going
to be a fantastic time and I cannot wait for it. Thank you.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: The previous speaker, Chris Tremain, is so full of
ideas that he could not even fill a 5-minute slot in the general debate. He sat down
before his time was up. Well, he is one of the members who are deserting the National
Party ship. He does not want to be a part of any potential future “coalition of the crazy”,
which Prime Minister John Key is currently out there negotiating.
I want to quickly touch on Minister Grose r’s performance in the House today. He is
off to Warsaw on his international speaking t our. I am sure he will be charging a hefty
appearance fee to appear at the Warsaw 19 th conference of parties negotiations. He said
he believes that New Zealand is doing real ly well. We are doing really well on climate
change! This is a Minister who has gutted the emissions trading scheme, has sat by
while our carbon price has utte rly collapsed, has devast ated our carbon forestry
industry, has made us a pariah on the inte rnational stage when it comes to climate
change, and has had enormous criticism fr om our Pacific Island neighbours about the
inaction of the New Zealand Government on climate change. He thinks he is doing
really, really well. But we need to acknowledge  that we are in the presence of a genius
when Minister Groser is in the House. Of course, he was involved in Closer Economic
Relations and said it actually should be called “Groser Economic Relations”. No one
else said that, unfortunately. That is what he said.
I say to this Government that it has been utterly negligent in its duties in the area of
climate change. It is an embarrassment to go from being a country that was clean, green,
and proud, that was seen as a leader in that area, to being seen as a pariah and getting
awarded the “Fossil of the Year” award for international climate change negotiations.
My concern is that when I look at where John  Key is taking the National Party, I do not
have any confidence that we can trust th e National Party to take climate change
seriously at all in the future.
We have got our Prime Minister, who is on reco rd as saying that he is suspicious of
climate change. He then said: “Well, no, no, I’ve always believed in climate change.”
But when he was caught in a moment of honesty, he said: “Well, if you believe in
climate change—and I am somewhat suspicio us of that.” We have his new BFF and
favoured political bedfellow, Colin Craig, w ho believes that climat e change is caused
by the circulation of the planets—the circulati on of the planets. Then we have Jami-Lee
Ross, an up-and-coming National MP, one of the young MPs in the National Party, who
yesterday, when he was doorstopped coming out  of question time, refused to state on
the record that climate change was real. It is a pretty simp le question to be asked as a
politician: do you believe climate change is real?

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: No.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Jami-Lee Ross refused to comment. I am a little bit nervous—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: David Bennett just said no.

items.speaker: MOANA MACKEY
items.text: Oh, David Bennett just said no. But that is David Bennett. He
is not one of the young up-and-comers in the National Party, to be fair. But that is
interesting—we will add him to the list of the “coalition of the crazy”, which does not
believe that climate change is real and which is suspicious of climate change. I am very
worried for the future of our planet and the fu ture of our country if  this Government is
re-elected in 2014—as it will not be.
13 Nov 2013 General Debate 14635
Going back to crazy Colin Craig, the future lead coalition partner in the “coalition of
the crazy”, his views on climate change are not the only interesti ng views he holds. He
came before the select committee hearing on marriage equality and announced a new
Conservative Party policy that none of us ha d been aware of in the past, which is that
the Conservative Party opposes unisex toilets—o pposes unisex toilets. It is one of those
hot political issues that no one  else wants to touch, that po litical parties shy away from.
His logic was that it is OK to treat people differently, so men’s and women’s ablutions
should be separate. He thought it was absolu tely appropriate that men’s and women’s
ablutions should be separate, so the Conservati ve Party opposes unisex toilets. This is a
future coalition partner of the National Pa rty if John Key has his way. That begs the
obvious question: does he have separate to ilets at home? Does he have men’s and
women’s toilets in his own house? I think that when that is the kind of tripe that is
coming out of the mouth of the preferred pol itical bedfellow of John Key, voters in this
country have every right to be very concerned about what a National-led Government, a
“coalition of the crazy”, would look like in 2014.

items.speaker: I say that the choice is clear
items.text: a coalition on this side of the House, which has sound,
evidence-based policies—it always cracks me up to hear the Prime Minister referring to
science. He is very selective in his choice of  science. He has ignored every single report
the Chief Science Advisor has provided to hi m, but when he thinks he can get out of
doing something, he will refer to science. You can have this side of the House, which is
evidence-based, which respects science a nd research, and which wants action on the
environment, action on climate change, and action on the economy, or  the “coalition of
the crazy” on the other side of the House, which is going to ban unisex toilets.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a pleasure for me to
take a call in the general debate this afternoon. I want to talk about the issues that matter
to my constituents in Maungakiekie, as we ll as to the people of New Zealand. But
before I do that, I want to just talk about my dad. He was my hero. He was a migrant to
this country. He passed away recently, and I just want to acknowledge him this
afternoon. He passed away playing golf last week.
I also want to mention Papaliitele Peter Fatialofa—last night I also attended his
funeral—and say just what a man of cour age he was. He was a man who stood for
values of community, of service, and of l oyalty, not only in the Samoan community but
also in the communities across New Zealand, and he is being buried this afternoon.
Last Friday was 8 November, and it was 5 years since National took office. It was
also my mum’s birthday and the day we buried my dad. I just want to say that this is not
going to be an overly political speech here today.  It is about some of the things that we
have done in the last 5 years and that the Government has delivered  on. It has been a
tough time, not just for my family in the last week but also for our country in the last 5
years. I think that is something that we can  all agree upon. The financ ial crisis did hit,
and regardless of assigning blame to whatever party or whatever pe rson, things needed
to be done in this country, and I am proud of some of the things that we have done to
address the issues around the economy, around jobs, and around the education system.
The recent household labour force survey fo r the September quarter did show that
over 2,270,000 people are employed in this country today. That is a large number. It is a
large increase on the corresponding figure fo r last year, and on the corresponding figure
for the previous quarter, to 30 June. What it means is that there are over 2.27 million
people who work in this country, who provide  for their families, and who are able to
better clothe their families, and that is a good thing. That is a good thing, regardless of
your politics. It is good to have people inde pendent of the State. It is good to have
people with the ability to look after their families, and it means that there are children
out there and there are families out there who are being cared for.
14636 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
Unemployment is down. It is at 6.2 percent.  That is a good thing, relative to what is
happening overseas—yes. Could it be lower?  Of course it could. I think we, as a
Government, are trying to address some of th e things that will bring the unemployment
rate down and to produce jobs in the di fferent industries th at New Zealand has
competitive and comparative advantages in. Whether that is in the mineral sector,
whether that is in the high-tech sector, whether it is in my local electorate, or whether it
is in high-value, value-added manufacturing, that is where our future jobs lie and that is
where I see our economy growing. Certainl y, I am hugely supportive of those local
businesses in Maungakiekie that contribute  to jobs and contribute to our economy,
especially the businesses of the local families in my area.
In terms of education, in 5 years—and I am  glad our former Minister of Education
Anne Tolley is here, in terms of the work that she has done in the education sector—I
am very proud, particularly of the amounts that are being spent in early childhood
education. Yes, members in this House can differ as to how that money is spent, but that
money is being spent on children—on children, toddlers, and young kids—who need an
investment in education, and $1.5 billion does contribute to parent-led centres. My own
daughter attends a playcentre in my local el ectorate, where there ar e also kindergartens
and other early childhood facilities that provide a really good start fo r kids to grow and
develop in our country. You know, compared w ith other countries in  this world, New
Zealand does offer one of the best education systems in the OECD and across the globe.
Thank you.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Can I say at the
beginning of my contribution that I acknow ledge Sam Lotu-Iiga and acknowledge the
passing of his father. I say to him that he has the sympathies and condolences of
members on this side of the House. I lost my mother 3 years ago. It seems incredibly
unfair, does it not, to lose someone so clos e to you at such a young age, and it can be
challenging to come back into the House and engage in the cut and thrust of politics.
Although I listened closely to what the member said and what he had to say about his
Government’s record over the last 5 years, I have to say that we do have a different
point of view on this side of the House, b ecause we are actually out there in the streets
listening to what New Zealanders have to sa y, listening to what people think about this
Government, and listening to the litany of  dodgy deals that this Government has
engaged in. The National Party is the party of dirty deals done dirt cheap. It will do a
deal with anybody, especially if it is a deal that gives prefer ence to its corporate mates,
and especially if it is a deal that will get it back into Government.
Let us look back at the long list of dodgy deals from National over the 5 long years it
has been in Government. It started off with Warner Bros, the American corporation that
came to New Zealand and created a phoney cr isis. It created a phoney crisis, and New
Zealand’s Government turned round and ch anged its laws. National prevented workers
from having the right to bargai n collectively in the film i ndustry because Warner Bros,
an American corporation, came along and de manded it. That was a deal that John Key
was ready to do.
Shell, another foreign corporation, came to  John Key and said: “We want you to get
rid of protesting at sea.” Na tional has never liked protesti ng at sea. Those members did
not want to get rid of the nuclear submarin es, and they took the first opportunity they
could to ban protesting at sea—a New Zealand tradition. And they did it because a
foreign corporation wanted to do a deal.
Then there was Skycity. National is prepar ed to increase the harm caused by
gambling, to increase the social costs that New Zealand taxpayers and consumers will
have to face, in order to do a deal that benefits its mates in the Australian corporation at
Skycity.
13 Nov 2013 General Debate 14637
It was ready to pay $30 million to Rio Tinto. It was not just a deal for its mates in
that foreign corporation; that was a deal to  prop up its failed asset sale programme. Let
us think about some of these policies that th is Government is promoting: selling off our
assets—assets that are profitable, assets that every single New Zealander benefits
from—so that just the privileged 1 percent get the benefits from  those profit-making
assets. And there is NZ Power, a good solid  Labour policy, which this Government is
dead against. Why? Because it would bene fit the consumers, the taxpayers, and the
workers of New Zealand, and it would not  benefit National’s mates—the people who
have bought up those assets and bought up those electricity companies.
Every deal this National Government does is in the interests of the few, the interests
of the 1 percent, and the interests of its mates. That is what those deals are all about. But
now it is about political deals, and it is about political deals to build the “coalition of the
crazy”. National wants to do a deal with Co lin Craig, the man who thinks that climate
change is all down to astrology. I do not know whether it is because Mercury was in
Venus, or what the story was, but somethi ng is changing our climate and Colin Craig
does not want to face up to the fact that it is man-made climate change. It has got
nothing to do with sunspots; it has got nothing to do with the alignment of the planets.
Then, of course, there is John Banks. The Prime Minister is always ready to do a deal
with John Banks. It does not matter how long he is before the courts and it does not
matter how many donations he received that he  did not declare, the Prime Minister is
ready to do a deal with John Banks. The Prime Minister is ready to do a deal with Peter
Dunne, the man he cannot even trust to be up  front about whom he did or did not leak
documents to.
This is a “coalition of the crazy” and New Zealanders have a real choice. They can
go for a solid, Labour-led Government, which is  working in the interests of taxpayers
and consumers and hard-working New Zealanders , or they can stick with the “coalition
of the crazy”, which is working for John Key’s crony capitalist mates. Those members
are not working for New Zealand; they are working for somebody else.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: It is interesting that the member
Iain Lees-Galloway brings up the Skycity convention centre, because for decades the
tourism industry has been asking various Governments and itself how it can get an
international convention centre in New Zealand. It  is true that as pa rt of that convention
centre there will be gaming machines. The New Zealand public in some way have found
comfort in the fact that the number of gaming machines throughout New Zealand has
decreased substantially over th e last 5 years. Across New Z ealand in bars and pubs the
number is gradually coming down, and, furt hermore, even though there are going to be
gaming machines in the new convention ce ntre, the number of gaming machines
throughout New Zealand is going to continue to decrease, which is good.
I am not necessarily pro-gambling, but I thi nk it is important to put into perspective
that this convention centre, worth about $400 million in private investment, is going to
be built in Auckland. It is going to attract international conventions, which we have
never held in New Zealand before. During th e construction phase there might be up to
1,000 people involved and during the operational phase many hundreds of jobs, and that
is what this International Convention Centre is all about.  So here is a convention centre
that produces jobs, and the Green Party and the Labour Party are against it.

items.speaker: Here is the common thread
items.text: they are not against just the convention centre, which
will produce jobs and growth; the Green Party and the Labour Party have at every turn
opposed the dairy industry expanding in Ne w Zealand. The Labour Party and the Green
Party oppose oil and gas exploration. They opp ose the exploration of minerals—that is
more jobs and growth out the window. So the Labour Party members, who are all for
jobs and the workers, apparently, are agains t the convention centre. They are against oil
14638 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
and gas exploration, which ha s occurred in Taranaki for 100 years with no problems.
They are against mining, which has occurred  on the West Coast for 100 years without
any problems. They are also against irrigation—for example, the irrigation of land in the
South Island. They are concerned about that . The Labour Party is railing against that—
more jobs and growth. Marine farming, a quaculture—every time some business person
wants to employ people and create a business and an income for himself and his family
or herself and her family, every time they propose a marine farm, the Green Party and
the Labour Party are against it—more jobs a nd growth that they oppose. Of course, in
the film industry they railed against Warner  Bros, which tried to stop the unions closing
down the Hobbit movies in New Zealand. Gerry Br ownlee and John Key stepped in, in
a way that was above board, and made sure that the Hobbit movies were actually filmed
in New Zealand. The Labour Party and the Green Party were against that.
What I am saying to the New Zealand publ ic is this: where once we had a Labour
Party that was all for the workers and that supported the beneficiaries, there is now a
Labour Party that will be only for the beneficiaries, because it opposes work. At every
opportunity to produce jobs—the  convention centre, marine farming, irrigation, oil and
gas exploration, the exploration of minera ls, the film industry—the Labour Party is
against that. There will be no work. It will be a party for beneficiaries, whereas the
National Party, as you know, has worked over the last 5 years with New Zealanders,
with businesses, with public trusts, and with all sorts of community organisations to
create jobs, to circle the wagons, and to work ourselves out of the recession.
We have gone through quite difficult times to a point where we now see
unemployment dropping and employment increasing. We are seeing interest rates being
held. We are seeing the best mortgage intere st rates for 50 years. We are in a position
where we do not want to put it all at ris k. We will not want to put the Labour Party,
which apparently is all for jobs but against all sorts of investment, in Government. I am
very proud to be part of the National Party, which has managed this economy over 5
years, and I cannot see why the New Zealand public would put all that at risk.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Actress, advocate, human rights activist,
international icon, social work er, trailblazer, JP, a friend to many in this House, the
name behind two questions in world trivia, and role model for the three Ps—politician,
prostitute, and public servant; roles that she felt were often interchangeable and
sometimes all played at the same time—Georgina Beyer first burst on to the scene when
she won Miss Personality in a drag queen contest. Her bubbly and straight-talking
persona made her an instant celebrity, from which she launched a long and tempestuous
career as a film and television actress—her modesty does not permit me to say when it
all begin, although her dazzling demeanour s uggests that there is more to come—
featuring on numerous television show s, including a starring role in Dancing with the
Stars, and earning a best actress nomination for her role in Jewel’s Darl.
But, undoubtedly, Georgina’s greatest infl uence came through her political career,
beginning when she rocked the pundits to become the world’s first ever openly
transsexual mayor in 1995, in Carterton, one  of the most conservative towns in our
country, defying the odds and overthrowing ma ny long-held stereotypes in the process.
More important, though, Georgina went on to earn the trust and respect of her
community with her straight-shooting and no- holds-barred approach to her job and her
public profile.
Always quick to latch on to a star on the rise, Labour encouraged Georgina to enter
national politics, and on 27 November 1999 she again made history as  the world’s first
openly transsexual member of Parliament, unseating the National candidate in a
landslide, and, again, in one of the country ’s whitest and most conservative rural
electorates, Wairarapa. Georgina says that  it was all much of a surprise, uttering a
13 Nov 2013 General Debate 14639
phrase that was heard all ar ound the Commonwealth: “Am I rea lly the first transsexual
MP? What about Maggie Thatcher?”. And yet despite winning one of the most
conservative seats in Parliament and representing its interests well enough to waltz back
in at the next election with an increased ma jority, Georgina was also the flag-bearer for
the gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender community, and led the House in promoting
prostitution law reform and civil unions. It was a pioneering and multifaceted role,
which turned her into a sought-after medi a commentator and international keynote
speaker on human rights.
In 2005 Georgina considered resigning from Parliament, disillusioned by the impact
that Labour’s foreshore and seabed  legislation would have on M āori, but she stayed on
to oppose what she called the homophobic rhet oric of groups like Destiny Church. She
eventually resigned from the House in February 2007.
In her time in this House Georgina served her many constituencies with passion and
with vigour. She is a knowledgable and fo rthright advocate for human rights, who
teaches us all to be strong in our beliefs, to be true to our history, to never back down
from a challenge, and to respect all those w ho want to be positive contributors to our
society, regardless of sex, race, creed, and gender. Georgina stared down all
examinations of her competence. She rose above the interrogations about her sexuality.
She handled the public perception with aplomb. She enj oyed a public profile that most
MPs could only dream of. And she did it all while holding the title of best-dressed
woman in Parliament for every one of her 8 years in the House.
Georgina recently became unwell with kidney failure, and so tomorrow we celebrate
her achievements at a special tribute even ing here in Wellington, organised by Louisa
Wall and hosted by Tariana Turia, where Ge orgina will be surrounded by friends, past
and present. And for those of you who can re member Georgina’s strident and powerful
opposition to the Destiny Church march on Parliament, please know that Brian and
Hannah T āmaki’s presence at the tribute to Ge orgina signals just how wide and
powerful has been the influence of this amazing woman.
Georgina, it is an honour to have you with us in Parliament today, and I am sure that
I speak on behalf of us all when I say th ank you for your wonderful contribution to this
House, to this country, and, indeed, to  the whole wide wo rld. You are truly a
remarkable woman, and today it is my honour to honour you on our behalf. T ēnā koe e
te tuahine. Tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I just want to acknowledge
Georgina Beyer from this side of the House as well. When I first came into Parliament I
remember your smile and your face around these premises. You are a friend to all sides
of the House. We wish you the best. It is  good to hear that things are happening
tomorrow and that things have progressed well. Best wishes for that. I also acknowledge
my colleague Sam Lotu-Iiga, with his father passing. It is very difficult to come into our
House and to express your personal circumst ances at the time. I think everybody in this
House can recognise and understand that. We  appreciate the approach the Labour Party
took, and especially Iain L ees-Galloway for his comments afterwards. I am sure Sam
appreciates that, and we certainly do, as anybody in this House would.
Getting beyond the personal, I guess, there is the politics that this place involves, and
a big part of that is the nature of the ba ttle you see between the ma in political parties
that this room represents. Today we are in the general debate, which is generally a time
where we have a good fight and attack each other. But it is a bit more subdued today
because of those earlier reasons.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: And they’ve got the B team from the National Party.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: But it is good to see Sue Mo roney here, my opposition from
Hamilton. When we think of the last 5 year s, it is important to think of, taking
14640 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
Hamilton, for example, what this Government  has achieved for the people of Hamilton.
I remember that when I came into politics the big thing for Hamilton was to get the
Waikato Expressway completed, the road of national significance—

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: Did you get it done?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yes, we have got that through and we are getting it built.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Are you just announcing it today? You’re announcing it again.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: The Ngāruawāhia section is due to be open soon. Sue Moroney
is saying that we are announcing it agai n. Well, we actually announced it, we are
building it, and we are doing it, unlike what ever Labour tried the last time it was in
Government.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: How are the jobs at Ruakura going?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Jobs at Ruakura—there will be more jobs at Ruakura as the
Tainui developments go ahead there. That ma jor inland port that you will see there will
be a major part of the development of Ha milton East going forward. Another thing for
Hamilton is that Hamilton has had a huge invest ment in its hospital, in the development
of the Waikato District Health Board’s ma in campus in Hamilton. Over $400 million is
being spent on the Waikato District Health Board. That is big money being spent on the
redevelopment of that hospital. I want to thank my colleagues from around the Waikato
who have lobbied for that over the years. I know that it is in Tim Macindoe’s electorate,
and he is very keen to see that money spent at that institution.
And then we go to education and we see th e great developments at Wintec with the
new buildings being built in Hamilton. We see the new schools being proposed for the
north of Hamilton East, and th at shows a growing area that  is being resourced and the
infrastructure coming in from this Government.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: You promised that 5 years ago, David. What happened?

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Sue Moroney was asking where it was 5 years ago. Well, Sue
Moroney, the Labour Party would not do anything 5 years ago. It is only since—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: You promised it 5 years ago.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Five years ago. What happened 5 years ago? The Labour Party
went to a piece of land and said: “This woul d be a great place for a school.” It never
promised any money, never promised any pr ocess, and never did anything. It had a
photo in the paper with Sue Moroney on a pie ce of land, saying: “Wouldn’t it be lovely
to have a school here?”. And then she comes into this H ouse and says that Labour
promised it 5 years ago. What a load of rubbish . That is a load of rubbish. The reality is
that the Labour Party did nothing. It deceive d the people of Hamilton, telling them that
there would be a school there when ther e was never an intention to build it.
[Interruption]

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Pardon? What did you say, Sue Moroney?

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: You promised it 5 years ago and it’s still not being built.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Yeah—5 years ago she was nowhere to be seen.
Broadband in Hamilton City—we are seeing broadband being put through that city.
The ultra-fast fibre network being put thr ough first in Hamilton and being delivered
through that city shows a Government investing in that city. I want to introduce
Hamilton today as an example to show what  this Government has done in 5 years.
Roads—we have built the Waikato Expressway and we are building the rest of it. The
inland port is going to go ahead under National.  We have got the internal ring route,
which is the road linking Hamilton North to the university. We have got schools coming
into Hamilton North. We have got the univ ersity and Wintec having developments on
their premises. We have got Waikato Hospital being redeveloped.

items.speaker: BARBARA STEWART
items.text: First, I must recognise Georgina Beyer. It is
always a pleasure to see former MPs return to the House. We in this House need to keep
13 Nov 2013 General Debate 14641
up with the times that we actually live in and be aware of what is actually happening.
People expect us to be aware of what is happening around th e country and to take some
action. The area of body art— tattooing, for some of us—i s very popular today. The
Government has basically got a role to play in ensuring that everyone who has a tattoo
is safe. If it does not, it is very costly to the health system. Other countries are actually
moving on this front, and it is time that New Zealand followed their example.
We have got a total lack of regulation in  this area. Many of the licensed operators
want action, and they are contacting me to ensure that some action is actually
forthcoming. What have we got now? Impor tation of tattoo equipm ent, including ink
with high levels of lead. Wh o cares? No one cares. We have got the onselling of tattoo
equipment to anyone and ever yone. Who cares? Again, no one cares. Of course, to add
to this, we have got unlicensed members of  the public actually practising their art on
unsuspecting members of the public.
We have to stop these products from comi ng in at the border. We do not know who
is importing these tattoo kits, how many ar e coming in, or who is actually buying these
tattoo kits. The only way to prevent th ese unlicensed tattooists—often called
“scratchers” around the industry— is to limit their ability to  get a tattoo kit. The only
agency that can make this happen is the Government, and it is time that action was
carried out.
I have got an email here from a tattooist , and he believes—and I totally agree with
him—that there should be some laws about th is. He said: “Resellers of skin penetration
equipment and pigments should be licensed in  some way as responsible resellers, so
they themselves are accountable. Reseller s should not be allo wed to onsell their
equipment to unlicensed practitioners. The pur chasers’ information should be required
on invoice statements, as well as their skin penetration licence. We do this for doctors
and we do this for dentists, so it is timely that  we did this for tattooists. We do not want
to see licensed studios that import their own equipment hindered by this law. They need
to carry on as they previously were.”
Does anybody in this House believe that the buyers of the kits that are advertised on
TradeMe and other internet sites with a reserve price of $1 for one kit with two guns are
actually going to be licensed? No, definite ly not. We do not know who is going to
actually buy that equipment. What has happe ned? The internet has become a way to
bootleg off these substandard products and i nks to unsuspecting buyers. So what have
we got? We have got unknown quantities of  gear coming in and gear of an unknown
quality coming in, and a vast amount of  ink. Ironically, you cannot buy inks off
TradeMe, but if you buy a tattoo kit, th e seller will ask you “Do you want ink with
that?”. And, of course, it is far easier to  get the ink. I know of people who are going to
the $2 Shop to actually buy the ink. How safe is that ink? It is not.
What we have got here—allowing unlicensed people to tattoo—is actually dangerous
to the population at large and, of course, to the industry, those people who are legal,
who are licensed, and who follow and carry ou t all of the requirements. I know for a
fact that many licensed tattooi sts spend their time fixing up the botched jobs that the
unlicensed tattooists have carried out. Usually, the initial cost is pretty similar, but the
quality is shocking.
What sorts of health risks have we got here? We are looking at infections, we are
looking at scarring, we are l ooking at nerve damage, and we  are looking at hepatitis C
and even HIV/AIDS. Urgent action is required by the Government.

items.speaker: Dr JIAN YANG
items.text: Wo hen hao xiexie. I am very proud to be part of this
National-led Government. Under John Key’s leadership and afte r National’s first 5
years in Government, New Zealand is in a much better economic position. Five years
ago National inherited an economy from Labour with a current account deficit at almost
14642 General Debate 13 Nov 2013
9 percent of GDP. Inflation was at 5.1 per cent. Homeowners were crippled by high
mortgage interest rates averaging 10.9 percent. The Labour Government’s spending was
up 50 percent and the economy was going nowhere but backwards.
Five years on, and how things have cha nged. The current account deficit is now 4.3
percent of GDP and inflation is now only 1.4 percent. Mortgage interest rates now
average 5.9 percent, so homeow ners have been able to pa y off their debt earlier. We
have reduced Government spending, despit e the global financ ial crisis and the
devastating Canterbury earthquakes.
Five years ago the economy was shrinking under a Labour Government. In the past
year our economy grew by about 2.5 percent, which is one of the highest growth rates in
the OECD, and we are on track to return to  surplus by 2014-15. Business and consumer
confidence is at its highest levels. Over the past 2 years more than 65,000 jobs have
been created, and unemployment is lower than in most developed countries. Our
economic programme over the past 5 years is clearly delivering for New Zealand.
The National-led Government has achieve d this positive economic momentum by
responsible fiscal management. We have not had to make major public sector cuts, as
seen overseas, and we have actually increase d our spending in key areas such as health
and education. We have put in  place plans that have made  steady progress in delivering
more jobs and higher incomes for New Zeal anders, and we have a busy agenda to
ensure that this progress continues, as our good work is not done.
Five years ago our trade with  our second-largest trading partner, China, stood at
about $8.2 billion. We have wo rked hard at continuing that  relationship. Now our trade
volume with China has reached $17 billion. Chin a is now our largest trading partner.
More important, New Zealand’s exports with Ch ina have more than trebled in 5 years,
from just $2.2 billion to over $8 billion. The National-led Government has also worked
hard to grow New Zealand’s tourism, which contributes almost 9 percent of our GDP.
The number of visitors from China has almo st doubled in 5 years, from over 120,000 in
As I am speaking, Minister Steven Joyce is visiting China to boost New Zealand’s
education profile. Currently, Chinese st udents account for 27 percent of our
international students and inject about $800 million into our economy. Education is now
our third-largest export to China, after dairy and wood.
Needless to say, I am very proud of what our National-led Government has achieved
in its first 5 years, and I am confident that  we will achieve more in the coming years.
You may be aware that last week the Prime Minister launched the New Zealand Story
project to help firms leverage off a str ong narrative about New Zealand’s uniqueness.
This will further enhance our brand in the world.
Before I conclude I would like to say that as a Chinese National MP I am very proud
of our Government’s continued support for New Zealand’s ethnic communities. We
recognise that New Zealand is increasingly diverse and we want to build a strong and
inclusive country where hard work is rewa rded. We also want to ensure that our
migrants and their families have access to information that would enable them to
integrate more easily, get ahead, and help th em have better lives in  New Zealand. That
is why we have—
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.

KAIPARA DISTRICT COUNCIL (VALIDATION OF RATES AND OTHER
